title: Fidelity Analysis of Adiabatically Driven Donor Spins as Two-Qubit and Ququart Systems
authors: Brian Michon, James Keppens, Ashutosh Kinikar, George Simion, Kristof Moors, Bart Sorée
abstract: Donor spin systems host a native Hilbert space whose dimension exceeds that of a qubit, meaning they can be used as qudits. Here we study a \ce{Si{:}P} donor spin system through leakage-aware randomized benchmarking (RB) of native ququart $\mathcal{C}_4$ and encoded two-qubit $\mathcal{C}_2^{\otimes 2}$ Clifford groups. We implement adiabatic ramps to operate electron dipole spin resonance (EDSR) pulses at the ionization point, where the electron is shared halfway between the donor and the interface, and to operate electron spin resonance (ESR) pulses near the interface, motivated by the sensitivity of the effective magnetic field to charge noise at the ionization point. By placing the electron near the ionization point only during EDSR control and using sufficiently long displacement ramp durations, leakage outside the computational basis is strongly suppressed, which is crucial for optimized qudit control. We find in our analysis based on leakage RB that $\mathcal{C}_4$ consistently achieves $\sim 40$--$50\%$ lower (lower-bound) error rates $\varepsilon^{\mathrm{LB}}_\mathrm{PT}$ with respect to $\mathcal{C}_2^{\otimes 2}$, due to its reduced circuit complexity. These results indicate that donor spin qudits benefit from genuine qudit operation as opposed to imposed encoded qubit operation.
summary: This work investigates using donor spins as qudits, comparing the performance of native ququart gate operations against those encoded from two qubits. Using leakage-aware randomized benchmarking, the authors demonstrate that the native ququart structure offers significantly lower error rates and is more resource-efficient than its qubit-encoded counterpart under realistic charge noise conditions.
main_problem: The study analyzes the fidelity of adiabatic driving protocols for donor spins when utilized as higher-dimensional quantum systems (qudits), comparing native ququart operation against standard encoded two-qubit operations.
main_result: Leakage-aware randomized benchmarking shows that the native ququart ($	ext{C}_4$) consistently achieves significantly lower error rates (40–50% better) compared to the encoded two-qubit system ($	ext{C}^{\otimes 2}_2$).
method: The fidelity is quantified using leakage-aware Randomized Benchmarking (RB), which accounts for state leakage outside the computational basis during adiabatic driving sequences.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a Si:P donor spin system, whose native Hilbert space allows it to function as a ququart ($d=4$). The control involves implementing Clifford group gates using both Electron Dipole Spin Resonance (EDSR) and Electron Spin Resonance (ESR) pulses.
key_observables: Average gate fidelity ($F$), lower-bound error rate ($\epsilon_{	ext{LB}}^{	ext{PT}}$), and survival probability $S(m)$ measured via leakage-aware RB.
important_parameters: The comparison is made between the native ququart group ($	ext{C}_4$) and the encoded two-qubit group ($	ext{C}^{\otimes 2}_2$), across varying adiabatic ramp durations ($	au$).
main_assumptions: Leakage outside the computational basis is suppressed by using sufficiently long displacement ramps, and charge noise is modeled as quasistatic with rare switching events.
figures_summary: Figures compare resource counts (pulse requirements) and show decay curves for fidelity metrics ($	ext{SPT}(m)$ vs. $	au$), demonstrating superior performance for the native ququart implementation.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the physical system and driving mechanisms, then details the use of leakage-aware RB to quantify gate errors, culminating in a direct comparison proving the structural advantage of using genuine qudit operations over qubit encoding.
why_interesting: It provides concrete evidence for utilizing higher-dimensional quantum systems (qudits) in solid-state quantum computing architectures by demonstrating superior error resilience compared to standard qubit encodings under realistic noise models.
